SOURCE: "Recitation-Augmented Language Models" (RECITE). Zhiqing Sun, Xuezhi Wang, Yi Tay, Yiming Yang, Denny Zhou (Google Research Brain Team and CMU LTI). Every page carries "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2023". arXiv:2210.01296v2, 16 Feb 2023.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/sun-2022-recitation-augmented-language-models.pdf

COVERAGE: I read all 79,687 of 79,687 characters (23 pages). I read the main text, ethics and reproducibility statements, and appendices A–G (prompts, prompt design, fine-tuning details, model descriptions, shot-count and FLAN-T5 analyses, Algorithm 1, Tables 6–7, Figs 7–17) in full. I only skimmed the references (pp. 10–14). Figs 4, 5 and 6 are plots and their values do not extract, so none of their numbers appear below.

CLAIMS
1. Writing out a passage from the model's own memory before answering ("recite-and-answer") beats direct closed-book answering on NQ, TriviaQA and HotpotQA, for all four models tested.
   number: NQ 5-shot EM: PaLM-62B 25.76 to 28.70; UL2-20B 10.16 to 14.16; OPT-30B 14.97 to 17.84; Codex-002 31.45 to 35.84
   setup: Table 1, closed-book few-shot prompting, 20 self-consistency paths, EM/F1. NQ uses the test split if it has labels, otherwise dev. TriviaQA and HotpotQA use "the first 1,024 data points". TriviaQA is 5-shot, HotpotQA 4-shot. NQ 64-shot (PaLM) and 16-shot (UL2) rows are also given.
   quote: "Standard-prompting (direct) 25.76 / 36.47(5) 10.16 / 20.17(5) 14.97 / 22.93(5) 31.45 / 44.75(5)" / "Recite-and-answer (20-path) 28.70 / 39.76(5) 14.16 / 23.13(5) 17.84 / 26.74 (5) 35.84 / 49.12(5)"
   where: p.7, Table 1
2. On TriviaQA the gain is small for strong models. The authors guess that trivia questions already carry the context that reciting would add.
   number: PaLM-62B EM 65.38 to 65.84; UL2-20B EM 48.73 to 53.42
   setup: Table 1, 5-shot, 20-path, first 1,024 examples
   quote: "TriviaQA Standard-prompting (direct) 65.38 / 71.85 (5) 48.73 / 54.32(5)" ... "Recite-and-answer (20-path) 65.84 / 72.10(5) 53.42 / 58.69(5)"; "improvements from recite-and-answer is more significant on smaller language models on TriviaQA"
   where: p.7
3. **Direct comparison with retrieval.** A single top-1 BM25 passage beats recitation for UL2 but loses to it for Codex. A ground-truth passage beats both by a wide margin, which shows how much headroom external evidence has.
   number: UL2-20B EM: none 10.16 / gold 41.02 / BM25 16.31 / recite 14.16. Codex-002 EM: 31.45 / 49.32 / 33.20 / 35.84
   setup: Table 3. First 1,024 NQ validation examples, 5-shot, 20-path recitation. BM25 is top-1 only, over the pyserini "enwiki-paragraphs" index. The ground truth is NQ's "long answer" annotation.
   quote: "Ground-truth passage 41.02 / 55.73 49.32 / 64.32" / "BM25-Retrieval (Top-1) 16.31 / 27.66 33.20 / 47.45" / "LM-Recitation(5) (20-path) 14.16 / 23.13 35.84 / 49.12"; "the classic retrieval model, i.e., BM25, is still a very strong baseline"; "stronger models (i.e., Codex) tend to benefit more from the the model's own recitation than BM25 retrieved context."
   where: pp.8–9
4. Fine-tuning PaLM to sample diverse "passage hints" (Wikipedia page, section and paragraph titles), then greedy-decoding each passage, adds a further gain on NQ.
   number: 5-shot EM 25.76 direct, 28.70 recite, 32.20 diversified; 64-shot 28.98, 31.34, 33.23
   setup: Table 2. PaLM-62B fine-tuned for "10,000 steps with a batch size of 64, which takes approximately 1 day in 64 TPUv4 chips" (App. C). The training data are synthetic question-hint-passage pairs, generated from 5 exemplars over top-retrieved Wikipedia pages for NQ queries.
   quote: "Recite-and-answer w/ diversified recitation (20-path) 32.20 / 44.02 33.23 / 45.29"
   where: p.8 Table 2; p.15 App. C
5. On multi-hop HotpotQA, "multiple-recite-and-answer" beats chain-of-thought with the same number of paths.
   number: PaLM-62B EM: direct 20.51, CoT 23.73, recite 26.46. Codex 28.32, 34.38, 37.11
   setup: Table 1, 4-shot, 20-path, first 1,024 examples. The CoT prompt is taken from Wang et al. 2022a.

6. Most errors come from bad recall, not from the reading step.
   number: TriviaQA UL2-20B: correct 53.42%, answer never recited 21.09%, recited but not extracted 5.66%, in some path but outvoted 19.82%

Method details for the note: recitations are drawn by top-k sampling and the answer is greedy-decoded from each one. The final answer is a "plurality/majority vote" (p.5).

LIMITS
- The authors concede (p.9): "updating time-sensitive knowledge for a pure LLM-based method requires training or fine-tuning the LLMs on the new corpus, which can be costly."
- Ethics statement (p.10): "unlike retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) models that can use external trustworthy corpus, all the intermediate steps in RECITE is generated by the LLM itself, RECITE may further enhance the existing biases".
- The abstract claims "new state-of-the-art performance in various closed-book question answering (CBQA) tasks", but no table compares against Atlas or any other open-book RAG system. The only retrieval baseline is BM25 top-1, on 1,024 NQ examples, for UL2 and Codex only.
- The ground-truth passage beats recitation by about 14–27 EM points (Table 3). Recitation leaves a large gap that retrieval of the right evidence would close.
- The appendix figures show recited passages that disagree with each other. For example, Fig. 14 gives four different home cities for the same band. The method relies on voting and does not verify recitations.
- There is no cost or latency analysis, even though 20 paths means about 20x generation. The authors cite "costly inference" only as their reason for subsampling paths.
- TriviaQA and HotpotQA use only the first 1,024 examples. Codex's size is unknown, and the paper reports GPT-3 hyperparameters "as a common educational guess" (Table 7).
- **Dated (my note, not the authors'):** the models are from 2022 (PaLM-62B, UL2-20B, OPT-30B, code-davinci-002), and there is no study of contamination or recency.

BUILDS ON: self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022b); chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022); few-shot in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020); closed-book QA with T5 (Roberts et al., 2020); the finding that CBQA scores reflect memorized training questions (Lewis et al., 2021); memorization and extraction work (Carlini et al., 2021; 2022); FiD-style aggregation of multiple passages (Izacard & Grave, 2021); retrieval-augmented baselines it positions against (Guu et al., 2020; Lewis et al., 2020; Izacard et al., 2022, Atlas); BM25 (Robertson et al., 2009) via BERTserini/pyserini (Yang et al., 2019a); Transformer memory as a retrieval index (Tay et al., 2022b).

CODE: the recitation prompt format, quoted verbatim from Fig. 9, p.18:
"Question: What was Beethoven's last symphony?
The answer to the above question can be found in the following Wikipedia page, section, and paragraph:
Answer: The year 1823 saw the completion of three notable works, ..."
Separators (App. B, p.15): "\n\n" between the parts of one exemplar and "\n\n\n" between exemplars. UL2 uses " ; " instead of "\n". Algorithm 1, the per-question error buckets, is on p.16.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1, p.1, is my pick. Its caption reads: "Illustration of evaluating (few-shot) open-domain question answering with (closed-book) direct generation ..., (open-book) retrieval-augmented generation ..., and (closed-book) recitation-augmented generation (ours)." It puts three panels side by side for the same question, so it shows the closed-book / retrieval / recitation split for "The knowledge gap" faster than prose can.
- Alternatives: Table 3 (p.9) as a compact numeric version of the same comparison, or Fig. 14 (p.21) to show four recitations that contradict each other.

PROBLEMS
- In Table 1, the NQ rows run the 64-shot (PaLM) and 16-shot (UL2) values into the 5-shot line. PaLM's 64-shot figure is confirmed by Table 2. That the 16-shot value belongs to UL2 is my reading of the column order.
- Table 5's check and cross column headers did not extract, so I used only the prose summary.
- Figs 4–6 are images with no numeric data.
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
